headline: One Scientist's Backyard Dream Becomes a 187,000-Acre Movement
meta_description: Doug Tallamy's simple idea—replacing invasive plants with native ones—has inspired over 52,000 people to transform private land into wildlife habitat.
summary_short: A University of Delaware entomologist turned a struggling farm into a thriving ecosystem. Now his Homegrown National Park movement spans 187,000 acres across America.
body:
On Doug Tallamy's 10-acre Pennsylvania farm, the transformation arrived quietly but unmistakably: wood thrushes returned to nest, luna moths reached record numbers, and more than 1,380 moth species now make their home where invasive plants once choked the land. When Tallamy and his wife bought the 300-year-old property in 2000, it looked green on the surface but harbored Japanese stiltgrass and mile-a-minute weed—invaders that starved pollinators. The solution cost almost nothing. "I think in the last 26 years we spent about $100," he recalls. "I simply go get seeds and put them in the ground." What emerged from that modest investment is now reshaping how Americans think about conservation itself.

Tallamy's insight struck deeper than any single backyard: nearly 80 percent of land east of the Mississippi is privately owned, and 135 million acres exist in residential landscapes. National parks, however precious, remain isolated islands. "In between protected areas is no man's land for most creatures," he argues. "Connecting those islands with habitat on private land is going to be the solution." This realization sparked Homegrown National Park, a nonprofit that registers people replacing conventional lawns with native habitat on a biodiversity map. The numbers tell the story: over 52,000 participants now steward 187,000 acres, figures Tallamy says are rapidly rising.

The movement's power lies in its simplicity and accessibility. Plant an oak tree and watch pollinators arrive within days. No yard? Try container gardening on a balcony. Unwilling to garden? Switch to an amber lightbulb instead of white to stop killing moths at night. Tallamy's half-million-copy bestsellers spread practical advice, but the real message cuts to survival: natural systems generate oxygen, manage watersheds, and sequester carbon. "Everybody requires healthy ecosystems," he states simply. "That means it's everybody's responsibility."
quick_facts: Doug Tallamy documented 1,380 moth species on his 10-acre farm
135 million acres of U.S. land are in residential landscapes
Nearly 80 percent of land east of the Mississippi is privately owned
